title: Chancellor accepts Labour has put a ‘lot of pressure’ on business and says helping entrepreneurs will be a budget priority – UK politics live
desc:
John Healey is expected to cut red tape requirements, particularly for smaller businesses

Kalyeena Makortoff is the Guardian’s banking correspondent.

CS Venkatakrishnan, CEO at Barclays, seems to have admitted defeat over bank tax hikes, which are expected to be a headline measure in Healey’s budget next week.

I recognise that the chancellor and the government has been entrusted with an important duty by the public and the people. And they have to balance a host of considerations. He [Healey] is the man in the arena, and I deeply respect the responsibility he bears on his shoulders and wish him well.

His long term goal is the same as our long term goal, which is to get growth.

So what is the chancellor now concentrating on? One could be forgiven for thinking him utterly unreconstructed: a party man and proud of it. There is no such thing as Healeyism, he says when the conversation turns to Anthony Crosland’s evangelism for the mixed economy: “I’m just Labour.”

“Just Labour” is exactly what the bond markets fear — and, indeed, it is what gives Kemi Badenoch hope of pulling off a comeback to rank alongside Lazarus and Bobby Ewing for utter implausibility.

Healey argued that his budget next week would refute the claim made by Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, about Labour not having the right policies to promote growth. In an article for the Financial Times, Haldane said Conservative policies were better for the economy, partly because they were more likely to support “cuts to business and employment taxes and regulation to unleash animal spirits”. In his write-up, Maguire says:

It was Haldane who also said, memorably and mercilessly, that the markets had concluded that this was a “traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”. At Westminster, this sort of criticism is at risk of curdling into thick and immovable consensus. What does Healey say to that? “I’d say to Andy Haldane,” he growls, fixing me with a cold stare, “speak to me next Thursday.” And, for the record, he speaks explicitly of “making an argument for how you bring welfare costs down” — albeit not via the “crude cuts” that were Starmer’s undoing.

Healey hinted that he was sympathetic to arguments that Labour should drop its plan to let younger workers qualify for the full national living wage. In his article Maguire says:

[Healey] is “acutely conscious”, too, of the “trade off” between an ever-increasing minimum wage — particularly for the youngest workers — and levels of employment.

He knows the many businesses who “want to employ young people” sometimes cite that upward ratchet as a reason they cannot.

Healey defended the part he played in bringing down Keir Starmer. Healey resigned from Starmer’s government over defence spending, and this contributed to the loss of support for Starmer in the parliamentary party that led to him standing down. Referring to this period, Healey said:

The country was ready for a change … Wherever you stood on the spectrum of the [parliamentary Labour party], there was a recognition that we needed a change.

We have a very rare moment now. We’re in the middle of a parliament, the second half of a parliament, and we’ve got a chance of a new hearing. People are at least willing to listen again … the Labour party is actually quite determined and disciplined, and in any party, the second half of a parliament starts concentrating minds.

title: French Counterterror Police Arrest 'Ultra-Left' Activist Over Limoges City Hall Fire
desc:
French Counterterror Police Arrest 'Ultra-Left' Activist Over Limoges City Hall Fire

French police on Tuesday arrested a 34-year-old man suspected of taking part in the October 17 arson of Limoges city hall, three days after the riots that gutted the 1883 building. The elite RAID unit's Bordeaux branch took him at 6:15 a.m. in a small, isolated house at Val d'Issoire, in the Haute-Vienne department, according to the Limoges prosecutor's office. The prosecutor called him a "person suspected in the fire." He is presumed innocent and has not been charged.

A source close to the case told Franceinfo he is an "ultra-left activist" already on the "fiché S" security watchlist. Some outlets first reported his age as 40; Franceinfo corrected it to 34. The prosecutor said investigators identified him through "painstaking" cross-checking of images and videos. ICI, the public radio network, reports that he is from the neighboring Creuse department and is suspected of earlier sabotage of TGV overhead lines and construction sites. His record was clean until an appeal court convicted him of violence against a police officer at an October 2024 protest in Guéret, a ruling he has taken to the Court of Cassation, so it is not final.

The Justice Ministry says he was not alone. Spokesman Sacha Straub-Kahn told ICI that "we are certain, from the images, that this person did not act alone," calling it a "manifestly concerted action" and putting the crowd in front of city hall at 500 to 700 people with "fairly substantial pyrotechnic means." No accomplice has been named or arrested. The only source for the ultra-left label is an unnamed one, and neither the prosecutor nor the ministry has said what role the suspect is accused of playing.

Custody, which began Tuesday, can run to 96 hours because the case falls under the special regime for organized crime. The investigation is run jointly by Haute-Vienne police and the national counterterrorism sub-directorate (SDAT). The national anti-terrorist prosecutor's office has not taken the case, but is following it. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said Monday that anti-terror prosecutors would soon decide whether to treat the fire as a suspected terror attack.

The fire itself began around 6 p.m. Saturday, when masked protesters entered the town hall and set it alight, according to the prefecture. Prefect Maurice Barate said the fire was set deliberately. Overnight the roof and belfry collapsed, and only the modern rear section was saved. Nineteen people were taken into custody that day, and four police officers were seriously hurt. Prosecutors opened an inquiry into destruction of property by dangerous means by an organized group.

Mayor Guillaume Guérin says the state left his police to face the mob. Guérin, of the center-right Republicans, told Sud Radio that national police ran out of crowd-dispersal grenades at about 3:30 p.m. and fell back, and that he saw about 700 infiltrators among a march of roughly 5,000 (a figure the outlet did not verify). He told Public Sénat that 400 rioters faced only 30 municipal police officers, and that the state is "in part responsible" for what happened. He has asked for a special rebuilding plan like the one for Notre-Dame, full state funding of what insurance does not cover, and has said he may resign if he does not get it.

Reacting to the arrest, Guérin said he expects the courts to be "up to the task" and wants the suspect jailed, while noting the presumption of innocence, because "he destroyed the house of all Limousins." He has secured a riot-police company for next Saturday, saying he needs national police and CRS officers "to maintain order." Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to visit Limoges on Friday.

title: UK Landlords Offered More Than Double Council Rents To House Channel Migrants
desc:
UK Landlords Offered More Than Double Council Rents To House Channel Migrants

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity.news,

British landlords are being offered thousands more each month to house small-boat arrivals than local councils pay to shelter vulnerable British families, a Daily Mail investigation has revealed.

The deals come from Clearsprings Ready Homes, one of three Home Office contractors operating under multi-billion-pound taxpayer-funded contracts.

In one south London case, a landlord was offered £4,500 a month for a three-bedroom flat he currently rents to Southwark Council for £1,790. That is an extra £32,520 a year, plus bills, council tax and maintenance covered for three years.

‘Are you a Labour MP? …because you’re a very sensible one!’ Michelle Dewberry agrees with Labour MP Graham Stringer that landlords shouldn’t be offered higher rents to provide accommodation for asylum seekers. https://t.co/nQ6KbsZY0u

— GB News (@GBNEWS) October 21, 2026

Landlords offered bumper rents to evict tenants and house small boat migrants as Labour accused of ‘outrageous racket’ in broken Britain https://t.co/YoOKKB5dQW

— Daily Mail (@DailyMail) October 21, 2026

The anonymous landlord told the Mail: "I already rent to Southwark Council, and they are able to offer significantly more than the local authority, which to me is bizarre. The council has a ceiling on what they are allowed to pay landlords like myself."

He continued, "For a three-bed flat I get £1,790 from the local authority to house families, while I would rent it to Clearsprings for £4,500 per month. I didn't go with them because it would have meant terminating my contract with Southwark Council and putting families at serious risk of homelessness. I am not prepared to do that. But many landlords just see it as an opportunity to earn more, and just go with them."

Here’s the kicker: The company, which has a taxpayer-funded contract worth around £7billion, is understood to be targeting landlords who currently provide accommodation to councils, students and vulnerable people, including those fleeing domestic abuse.

— Patrick Christys (@PatrickChristys) October 21, 2026

Clearsprings is understood to be targeting properties already used for council tenants, students and vulnerable people, including those fleeing domestic abuse.

The firm, run by Graham King (estimated fortune £726 million), houses around 30,000 asylum seekers and reported £62.6 million profit on £1.4 billion turnover in the year to January 2025.

It is one of three contractors (alongside Serco and Mears) with contracts originally awarded under the Conservatives and running until 2029.

The National Audit Office has previously put expected Home Office spending on the main asylum contracts at £1.67 billion for 2024-25.

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp called it "a day of shame for Labour" and said: "It is insane that illegal immigrants who have broken our laws, and some of whom go on to commit appalling crimes against women and girls, are being prioritised above law-abiding citizens who work hard and pay their taxes."

"Over 85,000 illegal immigrants have crossed the Channel under this Labour Government yet only seven per cent of arrivals are removed. This has led to a huge increase in HMOs and flats being used to house them - with over 93,000 people now in asylum accommodation," Philp further urged.

A Home Office spokesman claimed that the department pays a capped contractual rate and that "any amount above that is covered by the contractor and not taxpayers."

Officials pointed to hotel closures and claimed savings of more than £1 billion on asylum support since the election, along with 80,000 removals.

Meanwhile, Border Security Commander Duncan Capps has warned that nearly 3,800 migrants are currently waiting in camps between Calais and Dunkirk - almost double the usual number of around 2,000.

Nearly 4,000 migrants waiting to cross to Britain – double the normal amount -warns border security commander https://t.co/oJx5Fs3I5x

— Daily Mail (@DailyMail) October 21, 2026

Capps told MPs: "I think the French estimate at the moment is that there is almost 3,800 people between those two camps. Previously it was broadly about 2,000 between them." He added that larger boats and higher occupancy mean "it is only a matter of time till we have a mass casualty event in the Channel."

Crossings so far this year are down on last year's total, but the backlog in northern France shows demand remains high. Migrants typically make multiple attempts; French intercepts do not lead to detention, so the same people can try again.

Since Labour took office in July 2024, more than 83,000 people have crossed in small boats - more than the roughly 83,000 personnel in the British Army.

Total small-boat arrivals since records began in 2018 now exceed the combined strength of the Army, Navy and RAF. Former Royal Navy officer Chris Parry has described the intake under Labour as the equivalent of "six-and-a-half divisions of fighting-age men."

Arrivals have at times averaged one every minute during peak periods. The system processing them has been described by a Home Office decision-maker who assessed thousands of claims as fundamentally broken.

Speaking to The Times, the official known as J said: "At best 1 per cent of asylum seekers are genuine. There's almost no aspect of the asylum system that isn't either a massive fraud or just really dysfunctional. Nothing works as it should."

Common patterns include package claims from the same nationalities using near-identical stories, staged photographs, and networks charging thousands of pounds to coach applicants to claim they are gay or face political persecution. BBC undercover work has documented advisers offering fabricated evidence for sexuality-based claims.

The housing pressure is not new. Earlier this year the government signalled that every area of the country should expect to take a share of arrivals as hotels are closed and people are dispersed into residential property.

Projections have suggested migrants could account for 40 per cent of new UK homes by 2030 under current trajectories.

Local residents have repeatedly protested when HMOs or former military sites are converted for this purpose.

The current Clearsprings offers simply accelerate the same displacement dynamic with higher guaranteed rents funded through the contractor model.

The pattern is consistent: record crossings, low removal rates, an asylum system described by its own officials as riddled with fraud, and now private contractors using the resulting demand to outbid councils for ordinary housing.

British families on the housing list, students, and people fleeing domestic abuse are being asked to compete against a taxpayer-backed premium for people who arrived illegally.

The contracts were set under previous governments; the volume and the political choice to keep the system running at this scale sit with the current one.

Without a sustained reduction in arrivals and a higher removal rate, the housing pressure and the cost will surely spiral out of control.

title: "Mobilization Will Be Massive": French Govt Plans To Send Soldiers To The Streets After Admitting Failures
desc:
"Mobilization Will Be Massive": French Govt Plans To Send Soldiers To The Streets After Admitting Failures

French soldiers will take over guard duty so that police and gendarmes can be moved onto the streets for Saturday's expected protests, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told parliament on Tuesday.

Nuñez said troops from Operation Sentinelle, the anti-terror deployment, would replace internal security forces mainly on static guarding duties. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the same day that Saturday's mobilization of forces "will be massive," Remix News reported, ahead of a major protest planned for October 24.

— confrontation française (@confrontfr) October 17, 2026

Sentinelle was launched in January 2015 and keeps about 10,000 soldiers across France to guard against terrorist attacks, usually at places of worship, schools, tourist sites, railway stations and airports. It also covered the Paris 2024 Olympics and Paralympics. Nuñez described a post-holding role for the troops in this case, not a crowd-control one.

The government now admits it failed to contain last Saturday's riots. Lecornu acknowledged lapses in intelligence gathering, said police had been positioned too rigidly and said authorities chose not to cancel planned police leave, Reuters reported. He blamed far-left groups and framed the crisis as a choice "between violence and the Republic"; those groups say the government underestimated anger over living costs and declining public services. Nuñez told parliament: "I deeply regret what happened. I accept my share of responsibility." He offered his resignation, and Macron rejected it.

About 60,000 police and gendarmes were on duty nationwide on Saturday, October 17, when roughly 500,000 people marched against the cost of living (authorities told Remix 550,000; organizers claimed over 800,000). Nuñez called that too few for the large crowds of rioters and looters on the edges of the marches. He said police had "lost control" in some cities and admitted a "lack of anticipation." Riots and looting hit Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities, and in Limoges an arson attack brought down the roof and tower of the historic town hall.

— Remix News & Views (@RMXnews) October 17, 2026

The toll so far is large. Euronews counts more than 2,500 arrests and Remix more than 2,400 detained, while Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin put the number in custody at over 2,330, 70% of them adults. Almost 1,000 members of the security forces were injured. Alain Di Crescenzo, president of the chamber of commerce, said more than 2,000 shops were hit and put the damage at "hundreds of millions of euros." On Monday Lecornu asked regional authorities for "localised and partial curfews" and said nearly 200 Paris police investigators would comb footage to identify looters. Parliament is also setting up a commission of inquiry into the causes of the unrest. As we reported, 8 p.m. curfews followed in northern cities.

Nuñez is also considering banning demonstrations that have not been declared and could lead to public disorder. Declared marches could be caught too, he said, but only if organizers or their stewards give authorities reason to think things will get out of hand. For marches judged low-risk, routes should steer clear of public buildings and high streets, and intelligence services are to step up estimates of turnout, especially of the most radical participants. He said security forces need more "responsiveness and mobility" against "scattered" and "extremely mobile" groups, and told parliament: "We will be there."

The playbook has a precedent. In March 2019, for the 19th Saturday of the yellow vest protests, Sentinelle troops guarded sensitive sites so police could focus on order, and demonstrations were banned on the Champs-Élysées and in central districts of Bordeaux, Toulouse, Marseille, Nice and Rouen. Police made 31 arrests and issued 15 fines for entering banned areas, out of 2,322 street checks in Paris, NBC News reported. Macron brushed off opposition criticism of the army's involvement: "Those trying to scare people, or to scare themselves, are wrong."

Ministers of that period drew a line at confrontation. Armed forces minister Florence Parly said it was "hors de question" to put soldiers face to face with protesters, and said Sentinelle would relieve police and gendarmes of counter-terrorism tasks. Nuñez's description of static duties fits that model, though the government has not said where in the country the troops will be posted.

The unrest is also reaching the bond market. We reported this week that French 10-year yields hit 24-year highs near 5%, with the spread over German Bunds close to 160 basis points and Moody's due to review France's Aa3 rating, which carries a negative outlook. Earlier, we described the country as entering a "point of no return" as the riots spread.

title: NATO To Increase Black Sea Presence Following Drone Attacks On Shipping
desc:
NATO To Increase Black Sea Presence Following Drone Attacks On Shipping

Authored by Victoria Friedman via The Epoch Times,

NATO will send additional military equipment and aircraft to the Black Sea, following a series of drone attacks on shipping vessels in the key waterway.

Ships wait in the Black Sea in Constanta, Romania, on Oct. 15, 2026. Andreea Campeanu/Reuters

Allison Hart, NATO's principal spokeswoman, said in an Oct. 20 post on X that the assets will support surveillance, reconnaissance, and forensic activities.

The decision came after NATO ambassadors met at the North Atlantic Council, the defense alliance's main decision-making body, to discuss Black Sea security.

"We will continue to stand united and ensure that we are ready and able to address any threat and to keep our one billion people safe," Hart said.

NATO's military spokesman, U.S. Army Col. Martin L. O'Donnell, said that in addition to sending the radar systems, drones, and patrol aircraft, allies will send or have sent intelligence agents and teams to conduct forensic examinations of explosives used against shipping vessels.

NATO has not attributed the attacks to any country.

The added presence comes in response to several Black Sea incidents in which drones struck cargo vessels.

Earlier this month, a number of cargo ships were hit off the Bulgarian coast of the Black Sea in the space of one week.

On Oct. 13, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity was sunk, and the Chelsea 3, sailing under a Maltese flag, registered in Odesa, and Ukrainian-owned, was also struck.

Drones struck two other cargo ships in the same waters on Oct. 6.

Bulgaria said that Russia was likely behind recent incidents off its waters. Russia's ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, said at the time that she had no information from the Russian Ministry of Defense about attacks on commercial vessels.

Tankers Struck Near Romanian Coast

On Oct. 15, drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them both ablaze.

The vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea. It is a major export route for Ukraine.

Romanian President Nicusor Dan called the situation in the waters "serious."

"Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured, and missing, very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria," Dan said. "Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake."

Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the European Affairs Department at the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told Russian newspaper Izvestia on Oct. 20 that against the backdrop of NATO's increased reconnaissance activities in the Black Sea, "the risk of incidents, including unintentional ones, is indeed increasing."

Bulgaria, Georgia, Romania, Russia, Turkey, and Ukraine border the Black Sea, and it is a vital shipping route.

Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter, and Ukraine is also among the world's largest producers of grain and seed products - both use the Black Sea to export their goods. Consequently, the waterway has become a target for both sides in the ongoing war.

In recent months, Russian forces struck Ukrainian targets on the Black Sea, including the ports of Chornomorsk and Odesa.

Ukraine, for its part, has been targeting Russian grain and farming infrastructure in the waters.

title: The Turd-Eaters: France Gives Us A Lesson On The Pillager Class
desc:
The Turd-Eaters: France Gives Us A Lesson On The Pillager Class

Authored by Brandon Smith via Alt-Market.us

Over the years I have written frequently about what I call the “Pillager Class” and the “Producer Class” in an attempt to explore the reasons why certain people, groups and cultures always seem to turn to looting and destruction rather than building anything of value of their own.

It is a threat the west has been dealing with for thousands of years: We engineer and create and plan for the future, and instead of doing the same, the pillager class decides it’s easier to take what we have. Sometimes they are subtle like a parasite, and sometimes they’re not so subtle, like a swarm of locusts.

There are numerous theories on why this happens. Some think it stems from genetics, others from low IQ, others think it’s purely a cultural phenomenon, and some people argue that it’s a mere reactionary response to poverty. I suspect it’s a combination of all these things. At bottom though, it seems that certain groups are simply born with the pillager instinct; a subset of the populace perpetually stuck in scavenger limbo.

A good comparison to understand this is the classic “lottery winner” dilemma. Data suggests that around 70% of all lottery winners lose every dime they won in 5 years or less. It doesn’t matter if it’s thousands of dollars or millions of dollars; they can’t seem to keep their hands on wealth.

They go from cash windfall to bankruptcy and financial failure so quickly, winning the lottery is often treated like a curse rather than good luck. This happens because they are incapable of planning for tomorrow. Their brains are ostensibly stunted, and they can only think in terms of the present moment. They are doomed to live in poverty because they are incapable of growing beyond their most base desires.

The pillager class is very similar. You can take them out of the global ghettos, bring them to your home and give them every opportunity imaginable to improve their circumstances, and yet, they will always choose thievery and barbarism instead. The only thing that might change is the complexity of their crimes.

Somali daycare and medical fraud in the US is a prime example. Fake college degrees and the H-1B theft of American jobs by Indian scammers is another. The Muslim “Silent Jihad” – a strategy of invasion through false integration, is also a pressing threat.

These people aren’t thankful for the opportunities handed to them. They believe they are entitled. In every case they argue that it is Americans who should be grateful for the migrants on our soil, for it is they who “built our country” (Third world immigration to the US was highly restricted until the mid-1960s, so this claim is nonsense). They don’t care that their invasions will eventually kill the golden goose. Some of them WANT to kill the golden goose.

title: Israel Detains NY Congressional Nominee In West Bank Olive Grove, Sets Free After Learning Who He Is
desc:
Israel Detains NY Congressional Nominee In West Bank Olive Grove, Sets Free After Learning Who He Is

Some candidates kiss babies two weeks before an election. Brad Lander picked olives in the West Bank.

Lander, the former New York City comptroller and the Democratic nominee in deep-blue NY-10, posted this at 6:29am ET on Wednesday:

I've been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis & volunteers. We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nehalim in the West Bank.

The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn't a crime under any law I know. pic.twitter.com/r7B5Q3RvjY

— Brad Lander (@bradlander) October 21, 2026

Brad Lander speaks before being detained at the olive harvest. Video via The Guardian.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani chimed in, writing on X "Harvesting olives is not illegal. The occupation is," adding "[O]ther New Yorkers remain detained, and they must be released immediately ... The same Israeli government detaining them has committed a horrific genocide against Palestinians, killing more than 74,000 people over the last few years alone. "

Today, Brad Lander, rabbis, and other New Yorkers accompanied Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest. For that, they were detained by the Israeli government.

Harvesting olives is not illegal. The occupation is.

I am thankful that Brad has been released. But other New...

— Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani (@NYCMayor) October 21, 2026

In other words, a brief detention in a disputed olive grove has turned into an Israel-vs-New-York-City diplomatic spat, two weeks before the midterms and six days before Israel votes.

"Released Once The Matter Was Brought To Our Attention"

According to NPR, which had a team on the ground in Nahalin, Israeli forces declared a closed military zone around an olive grove near the settlement of Beitar Illit and detained Lander along with about 80 American and Israeli rabbis and activists. Two Israeli lawyers told NPR it was the largest mass detention of activists in the West Bank in at least a decade. The IDF's explanation for letting only one of them go was refreshingly honest:

"Regarding reports of the detention of a congressional candidate, we note that he was released once the matter was brought to our attention."

Lander put it his own way: he said he was released "with a 'warning,' apparently because of my public profile (I told them I wasn't even a congressmember yet, just a nominee)." The rest of the group, from the Rabbis for Human Rights delegation, was still being held at a police station in Beitar Illit hours later, according to the Times of Israel.

About That Map...

Here is where it gets interesting. The IDF told CBS New York that "harvesting in this area requires a request to be submitted to the relevant authorities in advance," and Israel Police said the group had entered an area near the settlement fence that needed approval. Lander called it "a bald-face lie."

The Times of Israel's US bureau chief then reported that a map handed out to Palestinian farmers by Israel's own Civil Administration shows the spot where the group was detained did not require prior coordination. Once reporters started posting the map, the IDF's new explanation was that the area isn't marked because Palestinians had never asked to harvest there before. Very reassuring.

Jerusalem's diplomats weren't having any of it. Israel's Foreign Ministry hit back a little before noon ET:

This was not about harvesting olives.
It was about harvesting headlines.

Brad Lander's latest stunt is nothing more than a calculated political provocation.

Lander traveled to a foreign country, deliberately entered a restricted security area, and participated in an...

— Israel Foreign Ministry (@IsraelMFA) October 21, 2026

To be fair, the ministry has a point about the optics. Lander's own posts framed the trip as an effort to shed light on the occupation, and a candidate who knows his district is safe has little to lose and plenty of cable hits to gain. The ministry's claim that his team was told ahead of time that coordination was needed hasn't been independently confirmed, but it hasn't been denied either. And Mamdani's "genocide" line is exactly the kind of thing that earned him bipartisan blowback over his Oct. 7 statement just two weeks ago.

Not all the criticism came from the left, though. Israeli MK Gilad Kariv warned (via the Times of Israel) that if someone doesn't stop "this madness, it will cause enormous damage to relations with Jews of the United States - and entirely justifiably so."

Who Harvested What

Lander's camp says a future congressman was hauled off for helping a farmer pick his own olives. Israel says it was a planned stunt in a restricted zone. Our summary is less so: by detaining 80 people and releasing only the one with a press office, Israel handed Lander and Mamdani a bigger platform than any olive grove could, and its own map undercut the explanation. With Israelis voting Oct. 27, Americans voting Nov. 3, and dozens of rabbis still in custody when this was written, we'll check back on whether the other detainees are deported, which would keep this story going right through both elections.

Then again, if harvesting headlines was the goal, it's been a bumper crop.

title: Ukraine's Anti-Graft Cops Raid The Central Bank... So Where's The Gold?
desc:
Ukraine's Anti-Graft Cops Raid The Central Bank... So Where's The Gold?

Ukraine's wartime corruption saga, which so far has swept through the state nuclear monopoly, the president's former chief of staff and the prosecutor general's office, has now reached the one institution that was supposed to be above it all: the central bank.

On Wednesday morning, detectives from the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), working with the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), searched the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) headquarters in Kyiv and the home of what the bureau coyly called "one of its employees." According to a law enforcement source cited by the Kyiv Independent, the premises searched belonged to Governor Andriy Pyshnyi himself, and MP Danylo Hetmantsev said as much publicly: the "employee" was the governor.

The NBU confirmed the searches and said it was operating as usual. By evening, Pyshnyi was on Facebook insisting that, per the court order, the criminal case concerns neither the central bank's activities nor his duties as governor, and that the searches turned up no evidence of wrongdoing by him or any NBU staffer. The central bank also denied rumors that he had resigned. Which, as anyone who has followed Ukrainian politics knows, is usually what happens right before someone resigns, or is resigned.

Follow The Sense Bank

So what are the detectives actually looking for? NABU hasn't said, but lawmaker Yaroslav Zhelezniak, who first publicized the raid, says it is tied to two cases: the Karpatnaftokhim petrochemical complex in western Ukraine, and the running of state-owned Sense Bank by outside individuals. Zhelezniak also called on Pyshnyi to step down.

Sense Bank is the thread worth pulling. The lender, formerly Alfa-Bank Ukraine and part of Mikhail Fridman's empire, was nationalized after Russia invaded. It has since become a recurring character in the Energoatom kickback probe, the largest corruption case of Zelensky's tenure. Prosecutors say a Hr 150 million ($3.4 million) bail payment for former Energy and Justice Minister Herman Halushchenko was routed through Sense Bank with allegedly laundered money, and in August they charged Zelensky's former deputy chief of staff Iryna Mudra, Sense Bank CEO Oleksiy Stupak and others over the scheme. The NBU, as supervisor, has been criticized for not stopping it.

The direct link to Pyshnyi: Sense Bank's former supervisory board chairman told a parliamentary inquiry that Vasyl Veselyi, a figure in the leaked NABU "Mindich tapes," was appointed to the bank on Pyshnyi's recommendation. Pyshnyi denies making any such recommendation. In those same tapes, Veselyi and businessman Oleksandr Tsukerman reportedly discussed influencing board appointments at the bank and talking to Zelensky's then-chief of staff Andriy Yermak about it.

That last name matters, because Pyshnyi got the job in October 2022 as a Yermak ally, after his predecessor Kyrylo Shevchenko abruptly resigned and then said NABU had accused him in a Hr 206 million embezzlement case at a state lender. Pravda reported in August that Zelensky was already unhappy with Pyshnyi and that his dismissal had been discussed. So two of the last two NBU governors have now had anti-graft detectives at the door. Not a great hit rate for the institution that also happens to guard the nation's gold reserves.

And as a bizarre coda, on the very same day Hungarian authorities detained György Matolcsy, Viktor Orbán's longtime central bank governor, whose son is the subject of a separate probe into corruption at the Hungarian central bank. Central bankers across the region probably had a quiet dinner tonight.

Speaking Of Reserves... Where Is The Gold?

Which brings us to the question nobody in Kyiv was asked today. To be clear upfront: nothing reported so far ties the NBU probe to Ukraine's reserves, and Pyshnyi says the case has nothing to do with the bank's operations. What follows is speculation, labeled as such. But if the central bank's supervisory function was compromised by people with access to the president's office, it seems fair to ask what else was sitting within reach.

On paper, the answer is reassuring. Ukraine's international reserves hit a record $57.7 billion as of Feb. 1 (unclear how much of that is US "donations") and monetary gold made up 8.5% of them, up from 5.7% a year earlier, thanks largely to gold's price surge rather than any buying spree. The World Gold Council puts Ukraine's holdings at 27.37 tonnes, unchanged through the second quarter, worth roughly $4.9 billion as of January per CEIC data.

Long-time readers will recall that Ukraine's gold has a habit of wandering off at moments of political upheaval. On March 10, 2014, days after Yanukovych fled, we flagged an entirely unsubstantiated report from pro-Russian outlet Iskra that the reserves had been loaded onto an unmarked plane at Boryspil and flown to the US, and asked whether the price of Ukraine's "liberation" was the handover of its gold to the Fed.

Was The Price Of Ukraine's "Liberation" The Handover Of Its Gold To The Fed? http://t.co/9loLVQl0dZ

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) March 11, 2014

The NBU denied it. Then in November 2014, then-Ukraine Central Bank chief Valeria Gontareva casually admitted on TV that gold was down to about $1 billion of reserves, which, on our math at the time, implied far less than that, and we wrote that Ukraine admits its gold is gone (Gontareva currently now faces Up to 12 Years in Prison and Confiscation of Property in Case Involving Collaboration with Russia).

Here is a transcript of the clip above:

  • 0:00 The NBU firmed the hryvnia by only 2 kopecks, to 15.75 per dollar. On the interbank market the dollar sold at 16.05 and the euro at about 20.
  • 0:14 The devaluation sent gold up 5% in a day. A gram of top-purity gold now costs 665 hryvnias, an all-time high, and the price has nearly doubled since January.
  • 0:38 Gold is disappearing from the NBU's vaults and is only a tiny share of the reserves. Gontareva said so herself on Channel 5 (5 Kanal).
  • 0:49 Gontareva says "Actually, practically, if you want to know, physically there isn't any. There's a small amount of gold bars, but it's literally, probably, up to 1%.".
  • 1:00 She didn't explain how it happened. Official NBU data show almost $1B of gold at the end of October, about 8% of reserves, or eight times what she says.
  • 1:20 Even by the official figures, holdings fell by more than a third in October alone. Gold prices are falling, so the NBU is selling into the drop and losing money.
  • 1:38 The gold was built up under former governor Serhiy Arbuzov, who decided in early 2011 to raise gold's share of reserves.
  • 1:57 Arbuzov, in an archive clip, says: "Roughly 21 tonnes of gold. That's several billion dollars… these are reserves that aren't subject to the changes paper money goes through, so the value will only grow."
  • 2:08 The bet made several hundred million dollars by late 2012, and the gold sat in a secure vault that journalists toured two years earlier.
  • 2:35 How the gold is now vanishing from the vaults is unclear.

A week later the central bank admitted the outflow and called it an "optimization of reserve structure," which is probably the most central-banker phrase ever coined for "it's gone."

NY Fed to Ukraine: "If you like your gold, we can keep it." http://t.co/RVgAVcqIqO

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) November 18, 2014

IMF data later showed holdings dropping to 23.6 tonnes in November 2014, a nine-year low, from over 42 tonnes at the start of the year. The official explanation was sales to prop up reserves, and by December lawmakers were turning on their own central bankers over it. Weeks later came the cherry on top: the NBU had been conned into buying painted lead bricks as gold, about $300,000 worth, allegedly with help from someone on the inside.

Ukraine Central Bank Conned Into Swapping Its Gold For Lead Bricks http://t.co/mYdQ6OUsDZ

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) December 22, 2014

So where is the gold now? Probably in one of three places, and here's where the speculation starts:

1. Where they say it is. The boring and most likely answer: the bulk sits in NBU vaults or, more plausibly given a war with missiles landing on Kyiv, in custody abroad. Wartime central banks routinely park bullion at the Bank of England, the New York Fed or the BIS, and the NBU has never published a bar list or a vault-by-vault breakdown. That opacity was a feature during the war. It looks a bit different on the day detectives are walking out of the governor's office with (heavy) boxes.

2. On the road. Ukraine's physical gold and cash do move, and we know this because one shipment got hijacked. In March, Hungary's counterterrorism unit stopped two Oschadbank armored vans near Budapest carrying $40 million, €35 million and nine kilograms of gold from Vienna to Kyiv, with Orbán accusing Kyiv of bankrolling the Hungarian opposition. Hungary's own tax authority later traced it to a documented Raiffeisen deal and closed the money-laundering case, and it is now Orbán, not Ukraine, facing a potential criminal case over the seizure. Still, it was a rare look at the logistics of state-owned precious metal moving across Europe in vans, and a reminder that gold, unlike a SWIFT transfer, actually has to be driven somewhere.

3. Pledged, swapped or lent. This is the one worth watching. Central banks under funding stress have a long history of quietly using gold as collateral, via swaps or leasing, while still reporting it as reserves. Nothing suggests the NBU has done this (or that it hasn't). But if the institution's governance was porous enough for outsiders to steer board seats at a state bank, independent confirmation that 27 tonnes are allocated, unencumbered and physically where they're supposed to be would seem like cheap insurance. Maybe the IMF, which has a seat at every Ukrainian table these days, could ask.

A Run On Trust, Not On Gold

For now, the more immediate risk is institutional rather than metallic. The NBU's independence is one of the few things Western lenders have consistently praised in Kyiv, and the IMF program and the EU's Ukraine Facility both lean on it. A governor ousted under a corruption cloud, with the president's office reportedly already wanting him gone, would hand critics of continued aid exactly the narrative they've been building since the Energoatom tapes leaked.

And if it turns out the case really does have nothing to do with the central bank, well, NABU just raided the head of the monetary authority of a country at war for a case unrelated to his job. Either way, someone in Kyiv is about to have a very uncomfortable meeting with the IMF mission.

title: How The NYT Hid Big Pharma PR Titan Jack Leslie In Plain Sight
desc:
How The NYT Hid Big Pharma PR Titan Jack Leslie In Plain Sight

Authored by Paul D. Thacker via The DisInformation Chronicle,

New York Times reporter Sheryl Gay Stolberg wrote one of the most hilarious, misleading pieces I've seen in recent months, castigating the NIH for a new vaccine injury clinic based on a leaked statement by Jack Leslie, a senior advisor to the PR firm Weber Shandwick which represents most major vaccine manufacturers.

I'm not joking. This is the journalism I get for my paid subscription to the New York Times.

Like most senior executives at the global PR firm Weber Shandwick, Jack Leslie makes buckets of money helping corporations sell themselves and their products to the American public. In the last handful of years, Weber Shandwick's clients have included the bulk of the global vaccine giants including Pfizer, Moderna, GSK, Sanofi, Novartis, and Eli Lilly.

But when he's not raking in oodles of cash repping corporate America, Leslie also takes on some unpaid healthcare positions as further leverage to market his lucrative pharma clients, such as heading the board of the NIH Clinical Center Research Hospital Board. The board met on Friday morning and Leslie's first order of business, I am told, was voting to castigate HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for establishing a new NIH clinic to study vaccine injuries.

Leslie then leaked his statement and the vote to Sheryl Gay Stolberg at the New York Times, whose story appeared within hours.

Stolberg's reporting - or whatever it was - failed to disclose that Leslie works for Weber Shandwick which advises pretty much every vaccine company on the planet. Here's how Stolberg describes him to New York Times readers:

Mr. Leslie, a former chairman of the global public relations firm Weber Shandwick, has advised the World Health Organization and numerous health-oriented philanthropies, and government bodies under presidents of both parties. He also chairs the board of the Elizabeth Glaser Pediatric AIDS Foundation, and advises global health institutes at two universities, Duke and Georgetown.

And here's what a tiny amount of suspicion and about 45 seconds on Google got me when I searched Leslie's background: his current biography at Weber Shandwick. Note the plaudits for Leslie's work advising vaccine manufacturers Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson, Merck, and Sanofi.

Back in 2022, I reported that Weber Shandwick had won a $50 million contract to embed their personnel at the CDC's vaccine center and advise physicians on COVID vaccines, while Weber Shandwick simultaneously had contracts with Pfizer and Moderna to promote their COVID vaccines. I caught one Weber Shandwick employee writing on LinkedIn that his duties at the CDC "focuses on boosting vaccination rates for flu, HPV, whooping cough, and COVID-19."

Days after my report, Senator Rand Paul sent the CDC a letter demanding that the agency turn over copies of their contract with Weber Shandwick, as well as the names of all of Weber Shandwick employees who were working at the CDC. A source inside HHS told me last year that, shortly after Kennedy was sworn in as HHS Secretary, Weber Shandwick's lucrative contract with the CDC was cancelled.

NIH established the Clinical Center Research Hospital Board in 2016 to advise NIH leadership on safety and regulatory compliance, and the NIH Director chooses the board members. Francis Collins appointed Jack Leslie to the board in 2022, and he was made chair in 2024.

The board's federal charter states that members must meet the following criteria: Nationally recognized leaders in sectors related to the NIH Clinical Center's duties, research hospital administration, clinical care, safety and quality, clinical and research compliance, or clinical research.

However, two individuals are chosen if they have been patients in clinical research studies.

I sent Francis Collins an email through his public relations rep asking why he chose Jack Leslie as a board member and how Leslie's background in pharmaceutical PR qualified him to be on the NIH Clinical Center's board. "Can you explain your thinking on that?" I asked Dr. Collins.

Collins did not respond to repeated requests for an explanation.

I also sent questions to Jack Leslie through his Weber Shandwick email asking who his current pharmaceutical clients are. However, Leslie also did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian appeared to add yet another stipulation to Tehran's growing list of demands that must be met if it is to get back to the negotiating table with the US.

Pezeshkian stated that some Washington-led sanctions must be peeled back before direct dialogue can resume again. He voiced that the constantly ratcheting economic warfare is closing diplomatic avenues, and so there must be a 'practical' easing of pressure to set an atmosphere of honest talks.

"Threats and sanctions must be removed in practice to pave the way for dialogue. We cannot increase the intensity of sanctions and pressure every day, close the avenues of interaction, and at the same time talk about negotiations," he wrote on X.

He is perhaps taking note of what's happening in US-Russia relations, where President Trump just waived the sweeping Graham sanctions package just ahead of when they were expected to be enacted. Trump also earlier this month facilitated the diesel release deal with Putin.

Out of these overtures has come an increase in direct Moscow-Washington dialogue. It seems Pezeshkian is holding out for the possibility of a scenario like this, depending on how desperate the White House becomes for a peace deal.

While there's no doubt that Iran's economy is under immense pressure, and average people are feeling the pain on a daily basis - especially given the plunging Rial amid runaway inflation - Iranian leaders say the country can endure in this wartime state of survival for at least years more.

The Pentagon and the Trump administration have been saying something different, however.

US Central Command chief Brad Cooper claimed last week that "The financial strain on Iran’s military has become so significant that there are reports of Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments to their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also is not paying its troops."

At various times over the last several months, Iranian officials have admitted the deep financial pain within society and impacting government coffers, also amid the US naval blockade which prevents Iranian oil from reaching global markets.

Yet Iranian leaders have remained defiant...

Iran has little hope that current talks yield progress--instead, it is preparing for US escalation, which it sees as likely. title: Oz Says HHS Is Deferring $1.2 Billion More From California Medicaid Funding
desc:
Oz Says HHS Is Deferring $1.2 Billion More From California Medicaid Funding

Authored by Troy Myers via The Epoch Times,

Medicare and Medicaid Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz announced in the Oval Office on Tuesday that the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is deferring an additional $1.2 billion in Medicaid funding from California over concerns of widespread fraud in its state healthcare programs.

The federal government's withholding of Medicaid payments to California now totals more than $3.3 billion.

"They just got the note, and we're doing that because of the growth of personal care services in California," Oz said.

"California has been growing that program 24 percent in the last three years. That is twice the rate of every other state average in the country. Impossible for us to understand how that could be so."

President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and independent journalist Nick Shirley joined Oz at the Oval Office event on Tuesday.

Trump administration officials credited Shirley for his work in exposing healthcare fraud in Minnesota last December, which launched him into the national spotlight as an independent government watchdog.

"I just was concerned about the well-being of our tax dollars," Shirley said during the White House event. "There's never been an incentive for anyone to ever expose fraud. In fact, when I expose fraud, instead of the mainstream media investigating the fraud, they investigated me, and people actually, in fact, wanted to kill me after I exposed the fraud."

After his video highlighted alleged fraud in Minnesota's daycare programs, Shirley made additional videos in New York and California.

In Oz's announcement Tuesday, he clarified that the deferment affects California's Medicaid payments directed to personal care services.

"Just that one little area where you're paying someone to carry groceries upstairs for your mom, which many of you would carry groceries upstairs for your mom for free, I would think, but in California, they'll pay you a lot of money for it, and it's actually run by the counties," Oz said.

Trump signed an executive order on March 16 to officially create an anti-fraud task force to be headed by Vance.

As part of Tuesday's White House event, Trump and Vance announced a $25 million Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program (WHIP), designed to reward Americans who help report misuses of U.S. tax dollars.

Under the program, citizens who provide tips that lead to a successful fraud conviction or a significant federal enforcement action are eligible to receive 1 percent of the amount of fraud discovered, Trump said.

The Justice Department will oversee WHIP, and Americans can submit tips online at fraud.gov.

"For the first time ever, there'll be an incentive for people to actually go out and make that change inside their own community," Shirley said about WHIP. "I hope by today, millions of people are empowered inside of the United States to go out and actually make a change inside your own community, and you'll actually be rewarded for saving America money."

Oz announced that the latest action against California's Medicaid program was on behalf of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who said on July 21 that CMS was withholding more than $867 million in Medicaid payments to California.

"Every dollar the federal government allows to be lost to fraud, waste, and abuse is a dollar stolen from American patients and the American taxpayer," Kennedy said at the time. "That's money that should be going to legitimate healthcare."

In May, Vice President JD Vance announced $1.3 billion would be withheld from California's Medicaid payments over potentially fraudulent billing patterns.

"We want to protect these programs for the kids and the families who need them," Vance previously said. "We want to ensure that the American taxpayer isn't getting fleeced."

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has called the withholding of funds politically motivated. His office did not respond to a request for comment about the latest deferment.

title: Hochul Weighs Ending $500 Million Medicaid Adult Day Care Program After Fraud Raids
desc:
Hochul Weighs Ending $500 Million Medicaid Adult Day Care Program After Fraud Raids

Authored by Chase Smith via The Epoch Times,

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has directed the state Department of Health to consider ending the state's Medicaid social adult day care benefit.

The directive came on the same day that state and federal investigators carried out a crackdown on providers suspected of fraud, and on the same day that Hochul announced 16 arrests in a separate auto insurance fraud investigation.

Hochul, a Democrat, stated at an Oct. 20 press conference that she had told the department to look at "all options to eliminate continued fraud, waste and abuse." Those options include phasing out the benefit and moving participants to other services for older New Yorkers. The department's recommendations are due by Dec. 31.

Social adult day care is a non-medical benefit offered through New York's Medicaid managed long-term care program.

It provides daytime supervision, meals, social activities, and personal care in a community setting. More than 400 programs serve about 45,000 Medicaid members at an estimated cost of more than $500 million a year, according to the governor's office. The federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) approves the benefit and helps fund it.

The announcement followed what the governor's office called a months-long investigation targeting more than 100 providers. The state Department of Health, the state Office of the Medicaid Inspector General, and the state attorney general's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit worked with the FBI and the federal Health and Human Services inspector general.

FBI agents and state officials raided programs across New York City on Oct. 20. CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz called the operation the largest enforcement action of its kind.

Hochul said she had gone to Washington to meet with Oz to discuss working together against Medicaid fraud, and that the investigation is targeting providers suspected of money laundering, kickbacks, and improper billing.

"We will find you, we will prosecute you, and we will hold you accountable," Hochul said.

At the same press conference, Hochul announced that a joint investigation by the State Police and the Department of Financial Services had led to 16 arrests in auto insurance fraud cases.

The cases involved nearly $500,000 in attempted fraudulent claims in New York City and Suffolk, Onondaga, Monroe, and Erie counties. Hochul said New Yorkers pay about $4,000 a year for auto insurance, almost $1,500 more than the national average, and that she expects the arrests and insurance reforms in this year's state budget to start lowering rates.

Reviewing Adult Day Care Claims

Regarding the crackdown on adult day care fraud, Hochul ordered the department and the state Medicaid inspector general to require health plans to review social adult day care claims before paying them and to pursue payment suspensions. A moratorium on new providers that the department imposed in July remains in effect until January 2027 and may be extended.

State Health Commissioner Dr. James McDonald said the department will advise Hochul on whether further reforms can deliver accountability or whether participants would do better under other services.

"Medicaid is a lifeline for millions of New Yorkers," Hochul said in a statement. "Protecting that lifeline means defending access to care and defending the integrity of the programs that provide it."

The program has drawn scrutiny before. A February audit by state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli found that managed care plans paid $2.4 billion for adult day care services from January 2019 through October 2024. Payments rose more than 141 percent from 2021 to 2023.

Auditors identified $285 million in questionable payments to centers for dates after at least one plan had dropped them from its network. That included more than $28.6 million to centers terminated for cause, such as fraud.

In one case, a center that one plan cut for fraud, waste, and abuse in 2021 stayed in the networks of 18 other plans and was paid more than $12.9 million afterward.

Auditors also found that a Flushing center with a legal capacity of 323 billed for 530 people on a single day in September 2022.

In its response to the audit, the Health Department said the comptroller's sampling method could overstate how widespread the problems were. The comptroller's office called that statement misleading.

Earlier this year, two people in Brooklyn pleaded guilty to a $68 million adult day care fraud scheme, according to the governor's office.

Asked whether ending the benefit would require federal approval and what services the participants would move to, the state Health Department referred The Epoch Times to the governor's announcement.

Hochul faces Republican Bruce Blakeman in the Nov. 3 governor's race.

Blakeman's campaign and CMS did not respond to a request for comment from The Epoch Times before publication.

title: What Could Democrats Do If They Win The Midterms?
desc:
What Could Democrats Do If They Win The Midterms?

Authored by Nathan Worcester via The Epoch Times,

Even as Republican campaign spending intensifies and the president holds rallies across the country for candidates, many forecasts still look grim for the party in power.

Observers from across the political spectrum predict that Democrats will retake the House, and maybe even the Senate.

What's on the agenda if Democrats win big?

Lawmakers and insiders have outlined a range of possibilities and priorities, including pushback against the Iran war, renewed attention to data centers and artificial intelligence (AI), and congressional investigations targeting everything from the Trump family's finances to the Epstein files.

Yet, President Donald Trump's vetoes may limit Democrats' effectiveness in implementing an affordability-focused plan touted by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), as could disputes within that party.

Still, some potential outcomes, such as even more delays or blocks of Trump's judicial and Cabinet nominees, seem baked into the cake - especially so if Democrats capture enough seats to bypass tie-breaking votes from Vice President JD Vance.

Pollsters Rich Baris and Mark Mitchell, both of whom predicted Trump's 2024 victory, see Republicans on track to lose the House and possibly the Senate.

During a Sept. 30 press conference, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said that his party was working to take the Senate in part to stymie the president's nominees for the Supreme Court and other courts.

Other possibilities - for instance, another Trump impeachment or two downstream of anticipated investigations - are far short of inevitable, at least partly because of the costs they may impose on some Democrats.

Impeachments

One man who understands the costs of an impeachment proceeding is Joe Cunningham.

The South Carolina Democrat entered the House after an upset victory in 2018, flipping a longstanding Republican district during a midterm election cycle that saw Democrats pick up dozens of seats in the lower chamber.

The lawmaker, who was a member of the moderate Blue Dog Democrats, lost his 2020 reelection bid to the current representative, Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.).

"I could argue that I lost my seat because of my impeachment vote," Cunningham told The Epoch Times, adding, "I don't have any regrets at all."

Rep. Joe Cunningham addresses the crowd at the South Carolina Democratic Party State Convention in Columbia on June 22, 2019. Sean Rayford/Getty Images

Retreading that familiar territory could hurt Democratic incumbents in purple districts, he said, arguing that Democrats should prioritize economic issues rather than an impeachment proceeding he predicted would "consume all the oxygen."

A Senate conviction - the step after impeachment that would actually remove Trump from office - would need support from two-thirds of that chamber. That's hard to imagine in even the rosiest midterm scenarios for Democrats.

Jeffries, though a vocal Trump critic who has accused him of unprecedented corruption, has not committed to impeaching the president.

President Donald Trump takes the stage during a rally at the Majestic Valley Arena in Kalispell, Mont., on Oct. 14, 2026. Travis Gillmore/The Epoch Times

Of course, Trump is not the only administration official Democrats might try to impeach.

Since the second Trump administration began, House Democrats have taken initial steps to oust Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, and Education Secretary Linda McMahon.

Attorney General Todd Blanche has also faced heavy scrutiny from congressional Democrats, who opposed his nomination.

He's also encountered criticism from his own party, including from Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) who accused Blanche of failing to comply with his legislation demanding the release of the Epstein files. A cosponsor of that bill, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), floated impeachment of Blanche in September.

That month, Massie also introduced articles of impeachment against Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, alleging his conduct of the Iran War has violated the War Powers Resolution of 1973. An early House recess short-circuited a push for a vote before the midterms.

Lindsey Cormack, a political scientist at the Stevens Institute of Technology noted Khanna's support for the Hegseth impeachment in an interview with The Epoch Times, saying he "will likely be targeted."

War Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks at Anduril Industries in Sparrow Point, Md., on Oct. 6, 2026. Madalina Kilroy/The Epoch Times

Investigations

The bigger - and broader - story might be investigations.

A flurry of subpoenas could hit those in and around the administration as Democrats seek to highlight alleged corruption.

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) have previewed possible probes into 1789 Capital, Donald Trump Jr.'s venture capital firm, and cryptocurrency deals involving the president and his family.

Despite the passage of the Epstein Transparency Act in 2025, redactions in them have driven controversy and could also spur action.

Khanna has said his fellow Democrats should make the Epstein files a major focus in the event they regain control of Congress.

The Justice Department has said the redactions in the files are intended to protect Epstein victims and their families.

Dave Spencer, host of the Practically Political podcast, advised Democrats to pick their battles carefully.

"If they launch too many investigations at once, the American people could begin to see it as overkill," he told The Epoch Times.

Data Centers and AI

Democrats may tackle two closely related issues currently in the spotlight - data centers and AI.

The proliferation of data centers, closely linked to the AI boom and backed by the president, has faced pushback in some local communities.

The Republican-backed Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation aimed at constraining the higher electric bills that hit some consumers after data centers arrive, passed the House but failed in the Senate before that chamber recessed.

Demonstrators protest construction of the Stratos data center in Utah's Box Elder County during a rally at the state Capitol in Salt Lake City on May 23, 2026. Natalie Behring/Getty Images

Democrats have touted a different data center bill, the GRID Savings Act, that would make the companies building out data centers pay for grid and transmission upgrades associated with the boom. GRID stands for Guarding Ratepayers from Increased Demand-costs.

Adam Swart of Crowds on Demand, a paid protester firm, weighed in on grassroots opposition to the buildout to data centers, describing it as "one of the strangest emerging bipartisan issues."

"Tucker Carlson-style Republicans and progressive Democrats increasingly oppose them, while the establishments of both parties largely support them. I suspect Congress eventually passes 'reform' that sounds restrictive but actually makes it easier for the industry to build," he told The Epoch Times.

AI could also spur action.

Amid the tech competition with China and AI-driven economic growth, Trump has cautioned against excessive regulation of the technology, which he has dubbed "super intelligence." Yet some lawmakers, including many Democrats, want more guardrails on those systems as some industry leaders publicly worry about AI safety.

Cunningham said that while he is not in line with the leftmost wing of the Democrats, AI regulation would be "more populist than socialist," and important for his party to address to win back support for 2028.

On Oct. 7, Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), who has worked with Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) on legislation to regulate AI, published a draft version of a bill that would impose a stricter liability standard on AI developers.

Other Priorities

Carmack, the political scientist at the Stevens Institute of Technology, told The Epoch Times she expects Democrats to apply pressure on AI and another contentious matter - immigration - through both legislation and spending negotiations.

Spencer too expects immigration to fuel spending battles between Republicans and Democrats.

Reconciliation bills passed by the GOP-controlled Congress have locked in years of funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement as well as U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

If Democrats perform well enough in the midterms, they could also step up their challenges to tariffs, food stamp cuts, the scope of military spending, and the Iran War, among other Trump policies.

Iranian-made Zolfaghar missiles are displayed at Azadi Square in Tehran on Aug. 2, 2026. Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images

The expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act (ACA), or Obamacare, premium subsidies, which triggered the longest government shutdown in history in late 2025, may come back into focus too.

Jeffries and Schumer have both vowed to tackle ACA restrictions championed by Republicans.

Legislation unveiled on Oct. 1 by the New York Democratic delegation, which includes both legislators, would roll back limits to the scope of those who can use ACA premium tax credits, a result of last year's One Big, Beautiful Bill Act.

"The ACA subsidies are a hugely popular issue, and Democrats would almost certainly make restoring them a priority," said Spencer.

Limits and Division

Insiders and experts see a narrow and highly political path to some action as the threat of a Trump veto looms over possible Democratic attempts to legislate on their affordability promises.

Spencer said Democrats could "advance popular legislation that would require Trump to either sign it or veto it."

Cunningham said Democrats could force hard choices through bills targeting the costs of everyday goods. He hopes the party will pursue legislation on prescription drug prices and anti-competitive practices by large corporations.

If Democrats rule Capitol Hill, they will still have to manage conflicts in their own camp.

At the Democratic National Committee's August meeting, dueling resolutions on Immigration and Customs Enforcement - one calling for reform, the other for abolition - underscored ideological divides within the party.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) at a hearing on Capitol Hill on March 5, 2025. Madalina Vasiliu/The Epoch Times

Republican control of Congress during the first half of Trump's second term was marked by conflict, both between different wings of the party and between the House and Senate.

Whether Democrats curb their infighting or not, the future looks explosive.

"This will be an adversarial two years in the run-up to the 2028 presidential elections," Cormack predicted.

Democratic dominance on Capitol Hill - and just how adroitly they tangle with Trump - would also give voters a yardstick ahead of 2028.

"If Democrats want to build a lasting majority - if they want to build some momentum going into 2028 - they've got to start making deliveries for people, for Americans who are getting crushed under this economy," said Cunningham.

title: Watch: Trump Indicates He Doesn't Yet View JD Vance As His Successor
desc:
Watch: Trump Indicates He Doesn't Yet View JD Vance As His Successor

This was awkward and unexpected, but on Tuesday in front of reporters' cameras, President Trump refused to commit to endorsing Vice President JD Vance for president in 2028.

He shrugged off a direct question about it, saying instead that Republicans first need to get through the midterms. Vance, standing behind the president in the Oval, seemed deeply uncomfortable when Trump noted that the two had never discussed such an endorsement - though he did call Vance "deeply talented".

“He’s a very talented person and he’s a very good person,” Trump said when asked alongside Vance in the Oval Office.

“I don’t think we’ve ever talked about it,” the president said, turning to Vance.

“No, sir. I said that too,” Vance chimed in. “Who would believe that?” Trump said, “I don’t talk about it with him. He doesn’t talk about it [with me]. It’s early.”

“We have to get through the midterms. We’ll see how it goes,” he added

Trump insisted it's too early, but the exchange raises huge questions about the Republican Party's future leadership, given other big contenders could be waiting in the wings, like Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The moment was all the more awkward for Vance given it came a mere day after the Vice President said he believed Trump would indeed endorse him if he ran for 2028.

Here's what Vance said in an interview on Monday, though he was obviously speculating:

“I think I would get his endorsement, but I also think there’s something to be said for people actually running their own race,” the vice president said.

“And because the president’s endorsement is so dispositive, you could absolutely see a scenario where the president says, ‘You know what? We need to let like this race play out and not preemptively prejudge the results.’”
